Every numeric format that deep learning has adopted in the last decade — FP16, BF16, TF32, FP8, INT8, FP4 — is the same decision made differently. You have a fixed budget of bits. Some buy **range**, the span between the smallest and largest number you can write down. The rest buy **precision**, how finely you can distinguish two nearby numbers. Spend more on one and you have less for the other.

That's it. That's the whole story. Once you see the trade, the zoo of formats stops looking like a pile of vendor acronyms and starts looking like a series of reasonable answers to one question, asked under changing conditions.

## What the bits actually do

A floating-point number is scientific notation in binary. Three fields:

$$\text{value} = (-1)^{s} \times 2^{\,e-\text{bias}} \times \left(1 + \frac{m}{2^{M}}\right)$$

The **sign** $s$ is one bit. The **exponent** $e$ says which power of two you're near — that's your range. The **mantissa** $m$, with $M$ bits, says where you sit inside that power — that's your precision. The bias lets a plain unsigned exponent field encode negative powers.

Two consequences worth holding onto:

- **Exponent bits are worth a lot.** Each one you add roughly *squares* your range, because it doubles the span of the exponent.
- **Mantissa bits are worth a little, predictably.** Each one you add halves your relative error. Not exciting, but steady.

Here is the whole family, drawn to scale:

```
                sign   exponent → RANGE        mantissa → PRECISION
FP32  32 bits    ▉     ████████ 8              ███████████████████████ 23
TF32  19 bits    ▉     ████████ 8              ██████████ 10
BF16  16 bits    ▉     ████████ 8              ███████ 7
FP16  16 bits    ▉     █████ 5                 ██████████ 10
E5M2   8 bits    ▉     █████ 5                 ██ 2
E4M3   8 bits    ▉     ████ 4                  ███ 3
```

Look at BF16 and FP16. Same 16 bits, opposite decisions. That difference is the most consequential fork in this entire history.

## Why FP16 kept blowing up

FP16 was the obvious first move. NVIDIA's Pascal generation shipped fast FP16 in 2016, and halving your memory while doubling your throughput is a deal nobody refuses.

Then people tried to train with it, and models started producing NaN.

The culprit is the 5-bit exponent. FP16's smallest normal number is about $6\times10^{-5}$. A perfectly ordinary gradient deep in a transformer might be $10^{-7}$. That value doesn't get rounded a bit — it becomes **exactly zero**. The weight stops learning, silently, and nothing in your loss curve tells you which one.

At the other end, FP16 tops out at 65,504. One activation spike past that and you get infinity, which contaminates every number it touches on the way back.

The fix that made FP16 usable was **loss scaling**: multiply the loss by a large constant, say $2^{15}$, before the backward pass. Every gradient shifts up fifteen powers of two into representable territory. Divide it back out before the optimizer touches the weights. Pair that with a **master copy of the weights in FP32** — so tiny updates don't vanish when added to large weights — and you have the recipe from the 2017 mixed-precision paper that made all of this practical.

It works. It's also a workaround, and it needs tuning per model.

## BF16: delete the bottom half

Google's answer, built for TPUs and now the default nearly everywhere, is almost insultingly simple.

**BF16 is FP32 with the bottom 16 bits thrown away.** Not approximately — literally. Same sign bit, same 8 exponent bits, same bias of 127. You just truncate 16 of the 23 mantissa bits and stop.

Two things follow. The conversion is nearly free, because it's a truncation rather than a re-encoding. And because the exponent field is untouched, **BF16 covers exactly the same range of magnitudes as FP32**. That $10^{-7}$ gradient? Fine. No loss scaling. No scale-factor bookkeeping. No 3am NaN hunt.

The cost is real: 7 mantissa bits gives you about two to three significant decimal digits, against FP16's three to four. BF16 is the *less precise* of the two 16-bit formats. It won anyway, because in deep learning it turns out that catastrophic failure comes from running out of range, while low precision mostly just adds a little noise — and stochastic gradient descent was already tolerating noise by design.

That's the lesson the field kept re-learning: **range is a cliff, precision is a slope.**

## The reference table

| Format | Bits | S/E/M | Max | Min normal | Digits | Bytes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FP32 | 32 | 1/8/23 | 3.4×10³⁸ | 1.2×10⁻³⁸ | ~7 | 4 |
| TF32 | 19\* | 1/8/10 | 3.4×10³⁸ | 1.2×10⁻³⁸ | ~3 | 4\* |
| BF16 | 16 | 1/8/7 | 3.4×10³⁸ | 1.2×10⁻³⁸ | ~2 | 2 |
| FP16 | 16 | 1/5/10 | 65,504 | 6.1×10⁻⁵ | ~3 | 2 |
| E5M2 | 8 | 1/5/2 | 57,344 | 6.1×10⁻⁵ | <1 | 1 |
| E4M3 | 8 | 1/4/3 | 448 | 1.6×10⁻² | ~1 | 1 |
| INT8 | 8 | integer | 127 | — | — | 1 |

\*TF32 is a compute format, not a storage format: it occupies a full 32-bit register and exists so Ampere-and-later Tensor Cores can chew through FP32-shaped work at reduced precision. In practice frameworks switch it on for you.

For a 7-billion-parameter model, that last column is the difference between 28 GB of weights and 3.5 GB — between four GPUs and one.

## Below eight bits, the trade splits in two

FP8 is where the single-format era ends. There are **two** FP8 formats, and the reason is the entire point of this article.

- **E4M3** — 4 exponent, 3 mantissa. Range up to ±448. Used for **weights and activations** in the forward pass, where values are well-behaved and you want every scrap of precision.
- **E5M2** — 5 exponent, 2 mantissa. Range up to ±57,344. Used for **gradients** in the backward pass, which span far more orders of magnitude and will happily overflow anything narrower.

Forward and backward have genuinely different statistics, so at 8 bits you stop pretending one format serves both. E4M3 also drops infinities in the standard variant, buying back a little range from bit patterns that were doing nothing useful.

## INT8 is a different animal

It's tempting to file INT8 next to FP8 as "the other 8-bit one." It isn't. **INT8 has no exponent field at all.** Its 256 values are spaced *evenly*.

That sounds harmless and isn't. A float's representable values bunch up densely near zero and spread apart as magnitude grows — which happens to mirror how weights and activations are actually distributed. An integer format spreads its 256 values uniformly across whatever window you pick, which means **you** have to pick the window: a scale factor, per tensor or per channel, mapping the real range onto ±127.

Now the failure mode is obvious. One outlier ten times larger than everything else forces the window ten times wider, and every ordinary value in that tensor loses a factor of ten in resolution. A single weird activation degrades the whole layer.

That one sentence explains most of the quantization literature. SmoothQuant migrates outliers from activations into weights, where they're easier to handle. Per-channel scaling gives each output channel its own window instead of one window for the tensor. GPTQ and AWQ decide *which* weights can afford to be crushed. NF4 reshapes the 16 available levels to match a normal distribution instead of spacing them evenly. Every one of these is fighting uniform spacing.

## The other half: why the hardware cares

None of this would matter if every format ran at the same speed. They don't, and the reason is a specific piece of silicon.

A **Tensor Core** doesn't process one number at a time like a CUDA core. It takes a small matrix tile and computes $D = A \times B + C$ in a single instruction — multiplying in low precision, accumulating in FP32 so error doesn't pile up. Since matrix multiplication is essentially all a transformer does, this is the whole ballgame: an order of magnitude more throughput than general-purpose cores on the operation that dominates the workload.

Which formats are fast is therefore a hardware question with a date attached:

| Gen | Architecture | Year | What it added |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | Volta | 2017 | FP16 in, FP32 accumulate |
| 2nd | Turing | 2018 | INT8, INT4 |
| 3rd | Ampere | 2020 | TF32, BF16, 2:4 structured sparsity |
| 4th | Hopper / Ada | 2022 | FP8, Transformer Engine |
| 5th | Blackwell | 2024–25 | FP4 / NVFP4, microscaling formats |

Read that column downward and you're reading this article's history from the silicon's side. Each generation is a bet on which trade the software would want next.

The same logic drives **2:4 structured sparsity**, introduced with Ampere. Unstructured pruning — zero out whatever weights you like — gets high sparsity but no speedup, because scattered zeros can't be skipped efficiently. So the hardware imposes a rule: in every group of four consecutive weights, exactly two must be zero. Rigid, only 50% sparsity, and the compression is real because the pattern is predictable enough to build a circuit around. Constraints you can exploit beat freedom you can't.

## What to actually do

- **Training:** BF16 mixed precision, master weights in FP32. This is the default and has been for years. Reach for FP16 plus loss scaling only if you're on hardware older than Ampere.
- **Inference:** FP8 on Hopper or newer. INT8 with per-channel scales elsewhere. INT4 via AWQ or GPTQ when you're memory-bound and can afford to measure the accuracy cost — and you should measure it, not assume it.
- **Debugging NaN:** suspect range before precision. Check whether something overflowed or flushed to zero long before you start questioning mantissa bits.

## Further reading

- **[Mixed Precision Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03740)** (Micikevicius et al., ICLR 2018) — the foundational paper. Loss scaling and master weights, explained clearly with real ablations. Start here.
- **[FP8 Formats for Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.05433)** (Micikevicius et al., 2022) — defines E4M3 and E5M2 and argues for the split.
- **[FP8 versus INT8 for efficient deep learning inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17951)** (van Baalen et al., 2023) — a direct comparison, and the clearest treatment of the outlier problem.
- **Deep Compression** (Han et al., ICLR 2016) — pruning plus quantization, from before any of this was standard.

---

Ten years of format design, and the argument never really changed. Bits are scarce, range fails loudly, precision fails quietly, and the hardware only goes fast on the shapes someone anticipated. The next format — FP4, microscaling, whatever follows — will be the same trade, made again, with the numbers moved around.
